 A Princeton University doctoral student was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after attending a neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C., according to the university and members of her research lab. Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, was detained by ICE on Thursday at an airport near Washington, D.C. and is believed to be being held in Chantilly, Virginia, according to The Daily Princetonian, the university's student newspaper. The Brody Lab, a neuroscience research group at Princeton University, said in a post on X that Xie was detained at Ronald Reagan National Airport while returning from the Society for Neuroscience conference, where she had presented a research poster. Rodney D. Priestley, Dean of the Graduate School at Princeton University, told Newsweek in a statement that, "News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community. "The University has arranged for Eva to be represented by legal counsel, and we will remain in contact with her legal team, her family, and colleagues to provide support," Priestly said. "We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.” Trump’s push for mass deportations has transformed ICE into a central force in the administration’s immigration crackdown, dramatically expanding arrests and removals across the country. ICE deported 483,200 people and made more than 491,000 immigration arrests in fiscal year 2026, the highest annual totals in the agency’s history, according to DHS data. Although the administration says its campaign is aimed at enforcing immigration law and removing dangerous offenders, federal data and independent analyses show that many of those arrested have no criminal convictions, while students and immigrants who entered through legal pathways have also been caught up in the crackdown. Xie emigrated from Shanghai, China, to the United States in 2016 and attended the Bronx High School of Science in New York, according to a 2020 profile in The Science Survey, the school's student newspaper. The profile said Xie initially struggled with English, but went on to become a finalist in the Regeneron Science Talent Search for research focused on using genomics to improve treatments for heart disease. "It's been a great shock to learn that ICE detained her on her way home. Eva is a valued colleague, and it's been a privilege to contribute in a small way to her research," Jorge Yanar, a fellow Princeton PhD candidate at the Brody Lab, told Newsweek Friday. "It's rare to see a graduate student arrive as prepared as Eva has and show so much initiative from the start. What I've appreciated most from working with Eva is the level of collaborativeness, kindness, and humility she brings to every conversation we've had. She's taught me a lot. We need her released and safely home as soon as possible." Newsweek has contacted ICE, and the Department of Homeland Security for comment via email outside office hours. The offices of New Jersey Senators Cory Booker and Andy Kim, as well as the government of New Jersey, have also been contacted for comment. Kim’s office and Princeton University declined to comment further on the case. The Brody Lab said Xie sent a message to her lab colleagues on Slack asking for help on November 19 before they lost contact with her. The lab said her lawyers were working to secure her release. "From my perspective, I would say that Eva is a ridiculously broad, ambitious, and generous scientist and colleague," Nathaniel Draw, another colleague at the Brody Lab, told Newsweek. "It's not typical for a student to have three advisors -- it's because of the breadth of her skills, interests, and work, which range from theoretical computer science to rodent physiology. She's also known among the PhD students here for her energy and generosity in organizing events to enrich the community, things like workshops by visiting science journalists." Carlos Brody, a Princeton neuroscience professor who advises Xie, criticized her detention in a statement to The Daily Princetonian, describing her as a “law-abiding student.” "Detaining her, with the intent of deporting her, makes no sense whatsoever. It is cruel, and it is our country shooting itself in the foot," he said. Xie graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024, with degrees in computer science and mathematics and a concentration in economics, according to her portfolio. Princeton Graduate School Dean Rodney Priestley told neuroscience graduate students that the university would remain in contact with Xie’s family, legal team and colleagues as the situation developed, according to an email obtained by The Daily Princetonian. It remains unclear what immigration status Xie held at the time of her detention. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Robinson and Emma Lee-Sang Update 11/20/26, 10:08 a.m. ET: This article was updated with additional information.
